title: Ezekiel 23:36–49
context: The LORD says to the prophet, “Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah?” and lists their abominations: idolatry, bloodshed, sacrificing their children, defiling the sanctuary, and profaning the Sabbaths, followed by the chapter’s strong imagery of welcoming foreign envoys and the LORD’s sentence through “righteous men” and a gathered company. The closing judgment imagery is violent and is described here only in general terms; it is prophetic allegory about the fall of both kingdoms, not a pattern for how any person should be treated, and readers in both traditions acknowledge that it is hard to read. Both traditions read the closing as shared ground about covenant unfaithfulness, and they note that the book elsewhere insists the LORD takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked (18:23; 33:11).

verses.text: The LORD said moreover to me: “Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah? Then declare to them their abominations.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Son of man, will you judge Oholah and Oholibah? Then declare to them their abominations.” Arminian readers note that the prophet is called to announce the charges.

The title “son of man” recurs (cf. 23:2).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet commissioned to declare God’s verdict.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a new section summing up the charges, and neither treats the title “son of man” as a point of disagreement.

verses.text: For they have committed adultery, and blood is in their hands. They have committed adultery with their idols. They have also caused their sons, whom they bore to me, to pass through the fire to them to be devoured.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says “blood is in their hands,” and that they caused their sons “to pass through the fire.” Arminian readers note the gravity of child sacrifice.

The charge is stated plainly and soberly.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the horror of offering children to idols.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that idolatry here involved real bloodshed of the innocent, and both read the charge with grief.

verses.text: Moreover this they have done to me: they have defiled my sanctuary in the same day, and have profaned my Sabbaths.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “they have defiled my sanctuary in the same day, and have profaned my Sabbaths.” Arminian readers note that the sins reach into worship itself.

The sanctuary and the Sabbath were signs of the covenant.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the profaning of holy things.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that idolatry and true worship cannot be combined, and that mixing them is itself a profanation.

verses.text: For when they had slain their children to their idols, then they came the same day into my sanctuary to profane it; and behold, they have done this in the middle of my house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “when they had slain their children to their idols, then they came the same day into my sanctuary to profane it.” Arminian readers note the hypocrisy of moving from child sacrifice to the temple.

Worship had become empty.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see religious outward forms covering great sin.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God rejects worship joined to injustice and idolatry (cf. Jer 7:9–10), and both read the verse soberly.

verses.text: “Furthermore you sisters have sent for men who come from far away, to whom a messenger was sent, and behold, they came; for whom you washed yourself, painted your eyes, decorated yourself with ornaments,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says the sisters “sent for men who come from far away, to whom a messenger was sent.” Arminian readers note that seeking foreign envoys is portrayed in the chapter’s strong imagery.

The point is political and religious courting of the nations.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see Judah adorning itself to win foreign favor.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as allegory of diplomacy and idolatry, described here only in general terms.

verses.text: and sat on a stately bed, with a table prepared before it, whereupon you set my incense and my oil.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes a table prepared, “whereupon you set my incense and my oil.” Arminian readers note that gifts belonging to the LORD were given to others.

The misuse of holy things is the point.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD’s gifts turned to the service of idols and alliances.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the verse charges Jerusalem with using what was holy to court the nations, and both describe the setting only in general terms.

verses.text: “The voice of a multitude being at ease was with her. With men of the common sort were brought drunkards from the wilderness; and they put bracelets on their hands, and beautiful crowns on their heads.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The voice of a multitude being at ease was with her.” Arminian readers note the careless revelry the LORD describes.

Foreigners are welcomed and adorned with bracelets and crowns.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a people at ease while betraying the covenant.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a picture of complacency and misplaced trust, without speculating about the specific groups described.

verses.text: Then I said of her who was old in adulteries, ‘Now they will play the prostitute with her, and she with them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD speaks of Jerusalem as long practiced in unfaithfulness, using the chapter’s covenant imagery. Arminian readers note the long history of unfaithfulness.

The pattern had become habitual.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see sin hardened by long practice.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as a description of persistent unfaithfulness, without repeating the imagery that follows.

verses.text: They went in to her, as they go in to a prostitute. So they went in to Oholah and to Oholibah, the lewd women.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD concludes the indictment of Oholah and Oholibah with strong allegorical language. Arminian readers note that both sisters are again named together.

The imagery is described here only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the shared guilt of Samaria and Jerusalem.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the close of the charges against both kingdoms, without repeating its imagery.

verses.text: Righteous men will judge them with the judgment of adulteresses and with the judgment of women who shed blood, because they are adulteresses, and blood is in their hands.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Righteous men will judge them.” Arminian readers note that the judgment is described as just, since “blood is in their hands.”

These judges may be those who carry out God’s verdict, though who is meant is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the sentence as just and hold the identity of the judges lightly.

Shared ground: both traditions read the judgment as prophetic allegory about the nation, and acknowledge that readers find it hard.

verses.text: “For the Lord GOD says: ‘I will bring up a mob against them, and will give them to be tossed back and forth and robbed.
verses.arminianNotes:
The Lord GOD says, “I will bring up a mob against them, and will give them to be tossed back and forth and robbed.” Arminian readers note the turmoil of invasion.

The language pictures the chaos of conquest.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s sentence carried out through human forces.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse soberly as the fall of the cities, and they keep the existing box at Judges 9:23 in view rather than restating it.

verses.text: The company will stone them with stones and dispatch them with their swords. They will kill their sons and their daughters, and burn up their houses with fire.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes the gathered company bringing violent judgment on the sisters, their children, and their houses. Arminian readers read this as allegory of the destruction of the cities.

They describe it only in general terms.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read it soberly as judgment on the nation, not as an endorsement of violence against women.

Shared ground: both traditions acknowledge, with care, that readers find this imagery hard, and both grieve the loss of children named in the verse.

verses.text: “ ‘Thus I will cause lewdness to cease out of the land, that all women may be taught not to be lewd like you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD describes the purpose of the judgment as ending the nation’s unfaithfulness in the land. Arminian readers note that the aim is to end the nation’s unfaithfulness.

The warning is addressed to the people as a whole.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse as a warning to God’s people about idolatry.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse within the allegory, not as a statement about women in general, and both describe it only in general terms.

verses.text: They will recompense your lewdness on you, and you will bear the sins of your idols. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “you will bear the sins of your idols. Then you will know that I am the Lord GOD.” Arminian readers note the recurring refrain of knowing the LORD.

Judgment aims at recognition of who God is.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God revealing himself through his acts in history.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the book later speaks of restoration and a new heart (cf. 16:60; 36:26), while letting this chapter’s sober ending stand on its own.
